raw_case_text: A 74-year-old known diabetic and hypertensive with good control presented to our institution with unsettling, high-grade fever for a week associated with retro-orbital headache, arthralgia, and myalgia. He was a farmer by profession and has had contact history with muddy water. He did not have respiratory or urinary symptoms. He was haemodynamically stable initially although urine output was low (<0.5 ml/kg/hr). Renal functions were markedly elevated, and bilateral moderate pleural effusions were noted in the ultrasound chest. Glycemic control was poor with initial random blood sugar of 350 mg/dl requiring an insulin infusion. Chest X-ray showed additional features of pulmonary haemorrhages. There were no skin rashes or lymphadenopathy. Blood was collected for routine cultures and Leptospira antibody test (microscopic agglutination test, MAT). He was started on intravenous ceftriaxone and methylprednisolone empirically with the suspicion of severe leptospirosis and pulmonary haemorrhages. Urgent haemodialysis was arranged every other day. Two days into the hospital stay, the patient acutely became drowsy and restless and electively intubated. Noncontrast CT brain excluded cerebral oedema or acute vascular events. Arterial blood gas analysis revealed a severe hypoxemia (P/F < 120). Lung-protective ventilation was continued although a fraction of inspired oxygen continued to escalate. Prone ventilation was opted approximately 14 hours a day. Pancytopaenia with hepatosplenomegaly was evident in the complete blood count and ultrasound abdomen, respectively. A multidisciplinary discussion with the general medical and haematological units was held. Persistent high fever with negative routine cultures and the rapid deterioration despite optimal supportive therapy pointed towards possible sHLH. Subsequent serum ferritin levels and trephine biopsy confirmed the diagnosis (Figures 1(a)-1(c)), aided by elevated serum triglycerides. After three doses of intravenous methylprednisolone, intravenous dexamethasone was commenced with intravenous etoposide twice a week. Sequential blood pictures and clotting parameters were suggestive of disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC). This was managed with transfusion of cryoprecipitate and fresh frozen plasma per haematological guidance. Persistent severe metabolic acidosis and severe hyperkalaemia were treated with haemodialysis under escalating inotropic supports (continuous renal replacement therapy was not available in our center). No structural anomalies or vegetations were detected in the 2D echocardiogram. The patient died following cardiac arrest on day 06 of the intensive care (day 15 of the illness). A highest MAT titre of 1 : 640 confirmed the diagnosis of leptospirosis posthumously. The summary of investigation results is illustrated in Table 1.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 74-year-old male farmer presenting with a 1-week history of high-grade fever, retro-orbital headache, arthralgia, and myalgia.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 74-year-old male farmer presented with a 1-week history of unsettling high-grade fever, retro-orbital headache, arthralgias, and myalgias. He was initially hemodynamically stable but oliguric with acute renal failure and bilateral pleural effusions. On hospital day 2, he acutely deteriorated with drowsiness and restlessness, requiring elective intubation and mechanical ventilation for severe hypoxemic ARDS. Despite lung-protective ventilation, prone positioning, intermittent hemodialysis, and escalating inotropes, he developed secondary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (sHLH) and disseminated intravascular coagulation, ultimately suffering cardiac arrest and death on ICU day 6 (illness day 15).
subjective.past_medical_history: Known history of diabetes mellitus and hypertension with good baseline control. Profession: Farmer with documented occupational contact with muddy water. No preceding respiratory or urinary symptoms.
subjective.review_of_systems: Reports retro-orbital headache, arthralgias, and myalgias. Denies cough, shortness of breath, dysuria, or gross hematuria. No skin rashes or peripheral lymphadenopathy noted.

objective.physical_examination: Upon presentation: High-grade fever, hemodynamically stable, oliguria (<0.5 mL/kg/h), no skin rashes, no lymphadenopathy. ICU day 2: Drowsiness, agitation, respiratory failure requiring intubation. Abdominal examination revealed hepatosplenomegaly.
objective.routine_investigations:
Admission labs: Marked elevation of renal function tests, random blood glucose 350 mg/dL. Complete blood count: Pancytopenia. Routine blood cultures: Negative. Chest radiograph: Features of pulmonary hemorrhage. Ultrasound chest: Moderate bilateral pleural effusions. Ultrasound abdomen: Hepatosplenomegaly.
Arterial blood gas (post-intubation): Severe hypoxemia (PaO2/FiO2 ratio <120), severe metabolic acidosis, and severe hyperkalemia.
Coagulation and hematology: Sequential blood pictures and clotting parameters demonstrated disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC). Serum biochemistry: Markedly elevated serum ferritin and elevated serum triglycerides.
objective.advanced_workup:
Non-contrast brain CT: Excluded cerebral edema and acute intracranial vascular events.
2D Echocardiogram: Normal cardiac structure, no valvular vegetations.
Bone marrow trephine biopsy: Confirmed hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (macrophage hemophagocytosis).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Confirmed severe leptospirosis complicated by severe pulmonary hemorrhage, acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), acute kidney injury, secondary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (sHLH), disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), and refractory metabolic arrest. Confirmed posthumously by microscopic agglutination test (MAT) with a peak diagnostic titer of 1:640. Routine bacteremia was ruled out.
Plan & Outcome: Empirically treated with intravenous ceftriaxone, pulsed intravenous methylprednisolone, insulin infusion, and alternate-day hemodialysis. Following intubation and diagnosis of sHLH, managed with lung-protective and prone ventilation (14 h/day), intravenous dexamethasone, intravenous etoposide twice weekly, escalating inotropic support, and blood product replacement (cryoprecipitate and fresh frozen plasma) for DIC. Despite maximal intensive care therapy, the patient developed fatal cardiac arrest on ICU day 6.
